projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with George T. Doyle was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran George T. Doyle, Mr. Doyle served in the U.S. Army with the 90th Infantry Division 359th Regiment, First Batallion, he served in the European Theater and highest rank was sergeant. He was awarded four Purple Hearts. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Doyle's home in Parma Heights, Ohio, on January 30th, 2003. George was seventy-seven at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Warsaw, Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: In '41, sixteen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, '41?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yes, I was bowling out on Arrana Avenue and I came home and found out about it. My folks were listening to the radio at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Continue on, tell me as much as you remember about that day?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Oh, well, everything that we read in the paper at that time, and I was just hoping the war would last long so that I could get into it. Not realizing at eighteen I would be into it up to my neck; but, we read the damage reports and all that type of thing, and not knowing where a lot of these islands were, that they were bombing, Midway and Wake Island and all that stuff, it made us look into history a little more to know where they were and what they were doing. The Phillipines were the other side of San Francisco is all I really knew at that time, but it did force the younger people to look into their encyclopedias and their world atlases and that type of thing to find out where things were in the world.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, let's see, you would have been a sophomore or junior in high school at that time?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Sixteen, sophomore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything for the war effort in those final couple of years in high school?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yes, I was active in the boy scouts and we did an aluminum drive, ten, twelve fourteen hours, one day and different parades and that type of thing having to do with the boy scouts. At school I don't think we did a whole lot for the war effort, except we did have a very strenuous gym program, which put us in very good shape. When we were in the service it was like basic training like gym, and that was a lot of help, and it had nothing to do really with scouting, you had to learn how to read a compass and follow a map and that type of thing, which is a lot of help in combat and training. I follow the war where we were suppose to go and where we were suppose to be.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did any of your classmates perhaps lie about their age and try to get into the service?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Not that I know of. But I did, one fellow I went to grammar school and high school with was six months older than I was, his birthday, I think was April -- no, had to be earlier than that. Anyway, we were graduating June and he was taken into the service and didn't graduate, he was taken in May. My birthday was in May and I got deferment to graduate and they deferred me for three months, otherwise, I would have been gone before I ever graduated from high school. That's the rate they were taking them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Depending upon your draft board how many they had, physical condition, whatever and the draft board that I was in evidently needed, needed people. And I don't know if I'd ever finished high school after combat if I hadn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, they were actually taking some kids before they graduated from high school?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Right, the one fellow that I was referring to, I still see him, he graduated from West Tech with my younger brother, three years younger. I went to his graduation, but he came back and he did go back to school and graduate. Some did, some didn't. Kind of lost track of each other, because most of the guys went into the service and we never saw each other again until we started to have class reunions. I still go to some of those, but it's not the same as you stayed together for fifty years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I was sworn in, what was it, on the 23rd of, September 3rd, something like that, actually reported for duty on the 23rd or 24th, I'm not sure, and I went from, it's in here. I went from Cleveland to Fort Hayes for one or two nights. And then we went to Camp Van Dornan, Mississippi, which isn't too far from the Mississippi River near Natchez. Had thirteen weeks of basic and three weeks of unit training, got a furlough and then joined the 90th Infantry Division. They asked for volunteers and I volunteered because I figured it couldn't be worst than Mississippi, and I think I was right. Mississippi in the winter, no place you want to be. Fighting in the civil war yet, we were still damn Yankees in the forties. Then I went from Camp Van Dorn by train, went south as far as Camp Gordon, Florida -- Georgia rather, then came up north through thirteen states and the District of Columbia to get to New Jersey. We came as far north as Cincinnati. We could see across the river, they put the engine on the other end, and that's when we went down into Georgia. They were trying to confuse the enemy. Well, they confused us too. I think it was thirteen days, something like that, to get from one area to the other, of course, we were supposed to everything all the way. We got there, the division had been activated in '42 and they had gone through desert training over Louisiana and all that, and then they found out that a lot of the guys were over age, bad physical condition, so they eliminated them. We filled in for them? They traveled from California to New Jersey, and then gave the guys furloughs back to California, that area. This is the government at that time. The division was formed originally World War One from Texas to Oklahoma National Guard, and that's where the T.O., and basically they drew from that area, the original division, but then I joined them at Fort Dix, we stayed there for a month, something like that, and then we went to Camp Kunifer for a night or two nights, got reissued equipment, then sailed out of New York, I imagine it was. We didn't always know where we were, and we took seventeen days going across the Atlantic in a convoy and we landed in northern England.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When would this be about?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: That would be March of 1944.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any memorable stories from that crossing, the Atlantic crossing?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: No, we just wondered how the tankers stayed afloat because they almost completely under water with the stormy seas. I was not seasick, but many of the men were, and we had nothing to do but lay around on a ship, and that type of thing, because we couldn't do anything, really. And stay either above or below deck, we couldn't all be one place at one time because we were at the full of the ship, that was the Affluent Castle that we went over on, and I understand that it was sunk by U-boats on the way back to the states, so, we're lucky once again. So, we landed in northern England and our regiment went to Wales, just across the border of England, oh, a thousand yards, something like that inside of Wales. And we trained there for a couple of months. The rest of the division was in England, and we didn't know why, but then found out that the first third battalion of our regiment was in Wales, made the invasion where the rest of the division came in D plus two, three, four, whatever, and so we were -- I was in combat, oh, two or three days before the division is credited with landing. First and third battalion of the 359 landed with the Fourth Infantry Division, which is a spear head division. It was the only division on that beach. General Theodore Roosevelt was still on the beach when I got there directing traffic and jumping ahead. He was scheduled to become our division commander and he had a heart attack and died. We had very poor leadership. We didn't get anything done right for the first couple of weeks and they were talking about breaking up the division and using us as replacements, we were so inept. And we got a commander and turned everything around and by the end of the war, Pat says we were one of his best infantry divisions. So, it's primarily leadership, the men were the same it was just the case of telling us where to go, organizing the artillery and that type of thing. One of the most memorable things right after the invasion, it was our first attack, one of the fellows got shot in the leg and he happened to be the lead man in the regiment. He took off running. Well, if you know how our artillery works, they fired five hundred yards ahead of you and keep increasing as you move forward. Well, we were not suppose to run. Well, we just ran into our own artillery and our casualties the first week or so were from our own artillery. But, this is what happens -- you can't, you can't govern that. I mean you're scarred or your wounded or something like that and you take off on a dead run and no way for artillery to know it because now you have communications between everybody and we didn't have that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was life like before you led the invasion?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Well, we were in seven man tents with a little heater in the center, and we fell out. We did calisthenics and we did some problems, that type of thing, and we marched, close order drill, that type of thing, for roughly the month that we were there. And our invasion maneuvers consisted of full field pack, everything we owned, and we marched across a stream about eight foot wide, about six inches deep. That was our invasion maneuvers. I've yet to climb down a cargo net. I happened to be fortunate when the L.C.P. was filled, they filled it up first on deck, then lowered over the side, and then when it comes back up to pick up more, then they have to climb down a cargo net. So, most of our guys never climbed a cargo net until they were shooting at us. But we took, we read about all the well trained troops. We were not well trained, we were poorly trained. That's why I take exception to a lot of the interviews, not this one, but when I read Ambrose books and stuff like that talking about how well organized and disciplined that everything was, that is not true. And the story can only be told by the people who were there. I have books over here in the bookcase written by Captain who landed on D-day and went through practically the whole war before he was wounded, and he tells a completely different than some of the others. I am active in our division reunion, and I still see fellows, I didn't know them at the time, but went through the same thing, the same areas and stuff like that, that I did. I have very little knowledge of the towns I was in because, you didn't look for street signs, you were out in the middle of the field and you had no idea where you were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were there any accidents in loading, going down the cargo nets?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I have no way of knowing that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There were several-- ________+

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: My group was put on the L.C.D.P. and lowered; so, we never checked to find out what was going on behind us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, what time did you go in on D-Day?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Approximately, ten, 10:30 in the morning.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What way would this be?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I don't really know. It would have been like three hours after each hour when the Fourth Division landed. They needed help and they unloaded us, and actually there were three battalions and the second battalion of our regiment, I don't know if they were scheduled to land or not, but anyway they hit, a mine and they had to swim ashore so actually they came in probably on D-Day, but without equipment and everything else. We were loaded down, we had two sets of everything. Two pair of underwear, two pair of pants, two shirts, an undershirt, a jacket, all this stuff, and we discarded most everything we could, and we didn't want on the beach; so, it ended up that they picked up our equipment. But they ended up without weapons and that type of thing which hopefully we hung on to. But when I came ashore there were bodies from the Fourth Division floating in the water at that time, and we had the easy beach. And I think what helped us greatly, We landed a mile and a half from where we were suppose to, and the Fourth Division commander, Barton, between he and Roosevelt, decided okay, we'll start here. Instead of reloading and going back out and moving, which would have been a disaster, trying to climb up a cargo net; so, we started the fight from there and that would change everything that we had known about maps and all our landmarks were different because we're a mile and a half away from. Basically the same as the airborne they landed in an area they weren't familiar with so their maps were useless. It was kind of a do your own thing type of thing, which is a great advantage as opposed to the German Army where if your officer didn't tell you what to do, you didn't do anything, and we were much more on our own for good or bad, but mostly I think it helped us a lot. The initiative of the Americans is a little different, everybody just lost.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This would be Utah Beach, correct?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you under, you have no way of knowing, were you under less enemy fire because you were in the wrong spot do you think?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Probably. The big -- I don't know what it would have been like if we landed in the right spot. But, where we landed, there was a roadway from the beach back inland, and on both sides of that it was flooded and they had telephone poles in the water for paratroopers, you know, get caught up and stuff like that. Anything that landed in the water recovered by machine gunfire and many of them drowned, but we had to go up that roadway; so, they had that roadway zeroed in, of course, there is no other place for us to go, but our casualties weren't too great getting in there because I think, because we weren't in the right place at the right time. Which was to our advantage.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about what you were thinking as you were heading toward the beach?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: That's a tough one because what anybody -- I think it was just one foot in front of the other and trying to get in there without getting killed and not knowing what you're going into and you knew, there's no way back, and you couldn't turn around and go any place because the ocean was behind you. It's a long swim back to England. I don't know that I had any great thoughts, just get my behind up there and get out of fire. We were still getting artillery fire and heavy mortar fire, which fires a longer distance and that type of thing. The Air Force, as I put in this sheet here, didn't do a whole lot because they either missed the pill boxes or didn't wipe them out, and it's been proven the naval gunfire was too far back from the beach, they were suppose to bomb on the beach so we have fox holes pre dug, a low spot to get into. That didn't work, they fired six miles inland. So, you know, we could all blame the other one, but, that's why generals get demoted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think it says in here that you saved a guy when you were going in?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yeah, we pulled in and, I think coast guard pilot, whatever, dropped the front end, that's the barge with the front end drops down and the first guy Andrew C. Nottin, Fort Nice, Arkansas, he was about six, two; six, three, and he went over his head. I was standing next to him and I grabbed his equipment and pulled him back in, and then they pulled us in another hundred feet or so, and then when we got off, it was still chest high to me. Had I stepped there, I'd gone two foot under water with all the equipment. When you get all that stuff soaked, you're pretty heavy. We did have life belts, but then on the other hand, we didn't, I didn't feel I wanted to be floating around out there, it's a bad place to float, you want to keep moving and no way you could, with all the stuff you carried, could you have been able to swim. Everybody had to carry extra ammunition, although you didn't use a mortar, you had to carry a mortar round so that way there's a hundred guys, we had a hundred rounds of mortar ammunition on the beach. We carried wire for, which would have been used by headquarters company for telephones and that type of thing. So we had to carry that. Everybody came in carrying much more equipment than they would ever need themselves. My version, we were expendable. They put divisions in there that had never seen combat and they saved the good troops for the follow-up. Make sense, but, you wonder whether you wanted to be one of the better troops or not. But they kind of figured that they would lose 'x' number of people the first day and therefore, better to get rid of your less trained troops, make sense, if you're not one of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, what happened on the rest of D-Day?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: We progressed, we were not attacking, we were, excuse me, still in reserve of the Fourth Division. I don't know which regiment, and we moved in about three miles, something like that, and spent the night, and the next day we started out on our own to not a major attack, but kind of clean up snippers and that type of thing, and we didn't go into our own attack until probably D plus 4, D plus 5, that's when the fellow got wounded and took us into our own artillery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was that actual first day of combat like for you?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Well, they call it the longest day but it seemed pretty short. I know that one fellow came over and he was all excited, he saw a leg laying all by itself on the beach. Well, what's your problem? He says, I never saw a leg blown off before. Well, this is a German leg, don't worry about it. The body is not going to bother you. Some people could accept seeing this stuff and others couldn't. As an example, in Private Ryan, they showed it basically what it was like and a lot of people can't stomach that, but that's what it is, war is not getting shot in the shoulder and put your arm in a sling. It's lay there and bleed to death and scream and holler and you can take it or you can't. I think what's caused most of the emotional problems, never seemed to bother me, I don't know lack of feeling or whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other little stories or incidents that you remember from those early days?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Well, we did pick up parachutes and use them for scarfs, which were very warm, they were nylon. I hung on to my life belt and used it for a pillow and that type of thing. Small things that you used to do on your own. My platoon sergeant was carrying a roll of wire, and he was struggling along and he was in front of me and I says, I'll take it. So, I took the roll of wire and he kept going, and then when we got off the beach, he says where the wire? I said, about three feet from where you handed to me. I wasn't going to drag something like it. We had it on the beach, I wasn't going to carry it all day. You're talking about A roll of wire about twenty-five, thirty pounds, plus your own ammunition and your own rations, which I think we had about a weeks worth of food, which had to weigh about ten, twelve pounds. We had about fifty, sixty pounds and I weighed hundred and twenty-six when I went in. The ratio wasn't there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what came next, then?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Well, from then on it's very, it's quite hazy, because the brain injury, which I suffered eight months later, that wiped out the memory as far as what towns we went to and that type of thing. But a few years ago I was over there, over in Europe in Normandy, and I went to the battle scene, sites that I had participated in. The tour guide, retired brigadier general's father was a regimental commander and he had all his notes, maps, etc., and he could tell us what company was there and what squad was there and that type of thing by his father's records; so, I've been in the field a number of places where I had fought. Changing the subject a little, I was in Luxembourg recently, and he took me to a place where I dug either in on one side of this road or the other and some of the slip trenches are still there; so, I got a lot of firsthand information about myself in the organization. Also, there was a young fellow that lived in Perrier, which is seven miles from the beach, and that was the first town that we took, and he started to say different things, he picked up on the beach, helmets, rifles, whatever, and now it's fifty something years later, I've been to his house a couple of times, he's got a museum of his own and, God, where were we. We had a reunion recently, and I can't think of where it was, anyway, they dedicated a room to him and pictures and stuff like that, that he has over the last fifty some odd years, he's been collecting, and people donated things to him and he's kept track. He has maps of just about everything the 90th Division has done, and he has been to the pentagon a number of times to get information. If anybody goes over there, he put you up with a family that you're compatible with. My wife and I, my son, who was thirteen, were put up with a couple that were school teachers. They figured a young boy, school teacher, it worked out fine. This small town takes in people, and you can't spend a dime. If you have post cards, they'll buy the stamps for you. You live with them, they won't accept anything at all. They take you any place you want to go, and I've stayed at their house now three times, and they stayed here a couple of times, it's reciprocal, you know. They took care of us and they were young at that time, in fact, the woman wasn't born at the time of the invasion. Her husband was, he was a little baby, and I met his mother and she described as well as she could the invasion to us because she was there with a small baby during that time and how the French hid their furniture and that type of thing in barns and covered it up and were under occupation for four years. It makes you realize that those people went through a heck of a lot. And then went the Germans pulled back, they took the cattle, everything they could carry, they took back as far as they could go toward Germany. They stripped that area completely. And, the only people that really benefited by the invasion of the occupation was Paris because it wasn't harmed and the people there by force of habit I guess, got along with the Germans and collaborated with them to a great extent. Well, the people in Normandy didn't and this is a farm community, a completely different type of people. And we have gone to a lot of small towns and the people have tailgate parties for us or they have something in the town hall, depending upon the economy of the town. You might get a glass of cider or you might get champagne. You might get chips and nuts or you might get a cooked meal, depending on the economy of those people. So, I have been one place in Seves Island, and my son laughed at me, how can you get surrounded on a piece of land like that, well, you forget that was one of the wettest years in history in Normandy, and we were circled there, and I think two or three hundred had surrendered, and right now it doesn't look like much, it's a river, not any wider than twelve feet, but at that time was probably fifty or sixty feet and the people will fall out there and carry over to the island on their back, if you want to go there and walk around and see this little island. But, things changed over the years and today we think of everything as, well, you can drive here, you can drive there, well, we walked. I don't know where you want me to go.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The town that you're talking about is Perrier, is that the town?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you were actually in there on D-Day, in '44, did you have much of an encounter with the French people?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: No, I can honestly say that I don't recall being anymore than a half dozen towns themselves. You're usually on the outskirts, you go around the cities, if they're house to house fighting in there, but a lot of times the Germans would pull back out of town, therefore, we went around the side or we didn't go into the city itself or the town itself. They don't have any cities. Most of those areas, they're a cross road with a half dozen houses, and that, might be three hundred people considered living in that area. And we still do hear from the couple that I stayed with.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, when did you get your first Purple Heart?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: On Hill 122. It's important to us because it had, it was 122 means 122 feet over sea level and from the top of that hill you had a view of the entire beach. The Germans had the hill. So, it ended up that we took the hill and consequently got surrounded, but we had to take that hill, and a lot of heavy fighting there because they had observation and would have been able to shelve the bullets, unloading equipment, food, whatever that we needed later, and I got hit, where did I get hit then. I got hit in the back, yeah, I was facing forward, the shell had to be behind me. I got hit in the back and actually it wasn't too bad, the first sergeant patched me up and then I never did leave the area. I got a Purple Heart that day. I got the combat infantry badge and I got my sergeant stripes in that area that day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that June 6th or after?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: No, that would have been June 12th, 14th, you really want to know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, no, no in relation to D-Day. So, approximately a week or so later?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, that was the first one. Was the second one soon after that?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: No, the second one was on the 5th of January in Dillinger, Germany. When the Battle of the Bulge broke out, we were in the third Army, we were south of that so we were already into Germany. This isn't a case that I shouldn't admit, but I had stolen, I should say, Czechoslovakian 81 mortar, and I got .81 millimeter mortar admonition from a supply sergeant and the platoon leader, my gunner and I went out with the mortar and we were just playing around, practicing. Well, I had also borrowed a German range finder and wanted to figure out how to use that. Well, we kind of made a mistake, we hit a truck convoy and they got mad and they fired back, and I was facing forward, I got hit in the stomach. My gunner was facing the other way, he got hit in the back and the lieutenant didn't get hit, he almost got court martialled because we were suppose to be in a holding position, not causing trouble. But, this is the American ingenuity, you saw something, you shot at it. So that was the first two. Then the third was in, just before the Prune River in Germany. After we closed the gap on the Battle of the Bulge and moved forward and they let the lead company go down a road. Our company was in reserve and as we came up to a certain point, they laid in artillery fire. Well, they had the first part, unit trapped, and so they hit us. And what I found out later was thirteen of us got hit and the other twelve died; so, I got hit in the top of the head, and that was my own fault too. I got some new men and I wanted to make sure they were down and try to dig in something and I stood up. I got hit, but they got killed; so, then I laid there from -- that was about six in the morning, which wasn't quite daylight, and then about six o'clock or seven o'clock that night as it's getting dark, I rolled over to get my canteen and got hit again in the back of the head, and I just laid there until artillery officer found me and took me back to, well, took me to division hospital, wherever it was, and then I was transported to the Liege, Belgium and the doctor that operated on me in Liege, Belgium that took some of the shell fragments out of my brain, it was a doctor that worked at Cleveland Hospital, which is now Metro. And, so, on the operating table we discussed the City of Cleveland, of course, I was in no pain at that time, but, I was conscious. And subsequently I went to Paris, then London area to hospitals and then came back on the Queen Mary, four and a half days on that trip, it's a hospital ship, and went to Halloran General Hospital on Long Island for one or two nights and then went to Martinsburg West Virginia and Newton D. Baker General Hospital, and I had a plate put in my head and had it taken out and put back in. I stayed there total from the day I got hit until I got discharged was a year and ten days in the hospital.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, your third and fourth Purple Hearts came on that?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: One day, about twelve hours apart.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Hit by sniper fire?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: No, that was artillery, I still have a piece of shell fragment in the cerebellum and a plate on the top and part of the skull missing in the back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay, well we jumped ahead a bit. If you remember anything else about the campaign in France?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Are you at all familiar with the Falaise Gap where the Germans were pinched off and it ended up that we were on the side of a hill and the Germans were coming from my left, and I thought I was the only one that saw them, and I had a .60 millimeter mortar and I opened fire on them, not knowing that this is a predetermined thing, and the artillery and everything else then started a fire, but, if you can picture it, they were coming from the left and there was a gap and that was closed by one of our companies of our battalion and the Polish troops. They met and I know, I knew very well, just died, the captain that made the initial contact with the Polish to close this gap. He ended up being a Federal District Judge in Los Angeles, and we closed that gap at Shamwah was the town, and it's called, Falaise is the other town, and I think a hundred and fifty thousand Germans were captured there, but because of a delay of the troops coming down from the north, I think another hundred and fifty thousand got back to Germany. This is the stuff that you read, now, well, so and so didn't move when he should have and his name was pronounced Montgomery, I think, that they stopped for tea or something, and they didn't close the gap so that was the hundred and fifty thousand troops that we had to fight again. We already had them trapped. I went down, this one fellow in my squad spoke German and we brought back hundreds of prisoners, they were perfectly willing to give up, but they were traveling and taking everything they could with them. Horse drawn wagons, carrying food, livestock and everything, and the Air Force came in and ship bombed them, and strafed them and everything, it smelled horrible, but there was thousands and thousands killed there. And the animals, they smell worst than humans. So, then we just, then from there, we until we got to Meds, it was much later, I have no recollection. I do remember one thing, though, we went down a road, we could see the Reims Cathedral straight ahead of us. We went off the road to the right and made a left turn and saw the Reims Cathedral from the side, we weren't allowed to go through Reims, basically that's what happened in Paris to, although we fought up the outskirts, the French drove through and the 28th Division just came over, nice clean uniforms, they marched through town, they didn't want us guys, needed to shave and smell like heck to walk into Paris. But then at Metz, which had never been taken before, there was a Fifth Division was up there before we were, and we relieved them. One incident, I'll never forget, I was given the job of going out to pick up dead bodies from the Fifth Division. Well, I felt my stripes, gave me a little authority so I assigned other people to do it. I wasn't into that. After they had been laying there for weeks and it rained all the time, we were up there and then we ended up crossing the river and cut the outskirts of Metz and the Germans were to our left and to our right, in fact, they were firing, what you call them bazookas, German Panzerfaust. They were firing down the road and at our tanks, and we had to duck because it came right down the road over our head. And the Americans came -- we didn't know that they were Americans, it was dark. We could hear stuff hitting the ground, we thought we were being strafed, that was the .50 caliber machine gun shells landing on us while they were shooting at the Germans. We were between two German forces and the Air Force was keeping them in town and our artillery was keeping them out of the town until finally I think it was the 30th Division that got credit for actually going into the city itself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then, where from then? Did you get a little break after that?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: The only real break we ever got was, I would say in division reserves which it would be still within heavy artillery fire from the front. No R & R as to, you know, what we know today or Viet Nam or Korea where you would go hundreds of miles back or Viet Nam they would go to, they would leave the country altogether and the same in Korea, they would go into Japan or something like that. We got nothing of that nature. I did get, the second time that I got wounded, I had been told I had a pass, a furlough back to the United States. I had to work on a hospital ship and I would get two weeks at home and then come back; so, I would be off for about a month. And then when I got wounded, I went to Division Hospital and I have, I still have the letter from my company commander asking that I not leave division because when I left division, I had to go to replacement depot and end up any place; so, they patched me up there, but then when the Bulge came, General Patton says I can be there; so, I was taken out of a hospital and instead of traveling with my division, I traveled a different route, truckload of us, and we joined the outfit in St. Fifth and that's when I first went into the Battle of the Bulge, actually the closing of the battle because our division wasn't there when it started, we went up there to close the gap, and I ended up getting there after the division. I saw one of my fellow sergeants on a truck frozen to death and stuff like that. Bodies thrown on trucks to get them out of the way. And, we went from there on through to February in many small skirmishes or large battles, that type of thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of any of that action during the Bulge?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Not really. I joined them in, oh, the 7th or 8th of December until the 26th, it was only nineteen days. And, I can't recall any incidents at all, but then when they say it ended and when, when you got someplace else, you didn't know that it had ended, and they still argue with us, the 26th, the 27th and stuff like that, but from then until February, I don't really have any recollection of where we were or where I was. I could make up stories.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, when that last time you were wounded was in February?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: February 6th of '45.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And do you know approximately where that happened?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Near the Prune River in Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You mentioned that?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: And I have been in that field and I met a German soldier that was also in that field that day and, on a trip, and I met and talked to each other as well as we could and he was willing to show me anything in Germany, I was on a tour, we couldn't leave. I had 242 days of contact with the enemy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the average?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: The average 12, 13 days, something like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's well over.

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: So, I was very fortunate and I've had problems with my health every since, but, I got all my pieces.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies with your outfit?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Not really. You learn very quickly, at least I did, not get too close to anybody. The one fellow that I pulled back out of the water when we were in basic training together, I knew him from there, and then my gunner and the mortar, and after he got hit, the same time I got hit in January, I never heard from him again. My platoon sergeant, I was close to him, and I wrote to his folks when I got home and I got a letter back, I'm glad you knew my son, etc., etc., didn't know he was killed, and it -- I wrote to three or four different people, I wrote to a woman whose husband was my platoon leader, lieutenant out of West Point, that was a very nice person. I got to know him in the two, three weeks that he was there and I found out that he was killed the day that I got wounded, and I lost my stomach for writing to people. Those letters, they don't cheer you up when you first get home. A lot of the fellows that weren't kept track of each other, their wives and their kids, they still come to the reunions and the families all know each other, and I've met fellows later, in fact, at one reunion I sat down and talked to a fellow and he was in my squad, it's like five in a squad. He had to be right because he could describe what I got from the company that I worked for. I worked for a publishing company and they sent me books, and he remembers me getting books on the front line. What are you going to do, you're not going to sit around and read a half a dozen books, and he remembered when I got packages from home with chocolate chip cookies and all that. I didn't know his name. I can't place him at all, but that was during a time period that is gone. They told me that I can have that brought back with hypnosis, but I'm not sure that I want to do that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, how long a period do you not remember?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Probably about, oh, four months, five months.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: My dad had a short period like that that he can't remember either. I lost my train of thought here. Do you remember a mail call, getting packages and letters from home?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yes. I can remember some -- I would remember getting books, because of all the things you needed was six books and that type of thing. The general letters, I got them, of course, but nothing that really comes to mind. Only when he brought back about the books and the chocolate chip cookies, I remembered that. I obviously got a lot of mail, that type of thing, but I don't, I specifically I can't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember writing back home?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yes, -- well, what we did was throw away our gas mask and use that container to carry your writing material, and that type of thing and rations, and one time I had to leave that, we were, I don't know what town it was, but, the Germans broke through and I looked up and saw a tank coming through this yard, and we were lower than the tank; so, I pulled the whole squad back into another area and the tanks didn't get us, they were firing over our head. Well, I let my muzak (ph) bag, my mortar, my site and everything else in that hole. They told me I would be court martialled, I wasn't concerned with that, but when we attacked back, went to that hole and picked up all my equipment. But I did write back. I hung on to letters until I answered them, and then I tore the letters up, that type of thing. And as far as, you couldn't write much about where you were and what you were doing because the sensor would cut it out anyway. But my father, having served in the same general area in France, had a pretty good idea where we were, all I had to tell him was that, where I got wounded or something like that, and he knew that was in Verdon and that type of thing. We all saw this and were able to do something like that -- but you couldn't be blatant about and say where you were. And they had maps and I got newspapers that showed approximately where outfits were. So, my father could follow it pretty well, but, it worked out all right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Of those rare times that you might have gotten a break from combat, do you remember doing anything for entertainment?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Only when I was in the Division Hospital, there was a USO show there, and I don't remember who the people were and that's the only show I ever saw while I was there. It's the only time that I ever got any doughnuts. I know they came up to the front line and all that stuff, but I never saw them. I think they came to the Air Force and that type of thing, or, they came outfits when they were back a mile or two from combat. Because, your heavy artillery would travel twenty or thirty miles and brave as they were, they're not going up there, they weren't getting that fifty bucks a month, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, did the guys do anything in particular even when they're on the line, make up songs or anything like that?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Not that I can recall, no, bitch and crab, that type of thing. I did from Germany, had a pass back to Paris, and I had no money, and we all sent our money home; so, I got, I didn't smoke, I still don't. So, I gave my cigarettes away to different people in the outfit and candy bars and stuff like that, that I didn't want; so, it came time to get, to go back to Paris, I asked for cigarettes and candy bars and whatever. I spent three days in Paris, I sold the stuff to dancers in a bar in Paris, the owner of which was an American G.I. from World War I that stayed over there and married a French girl, and I lived pretty good for three days on my I.O.U.'s from past ingenuity. But, then, we had to take, you know, an open truck all the way from Paris up into Germany, you wonder if it was worth it, freezing to death.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you on V.E. Day, probably in the hospital, right?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I was home on furlough, and our scout troop had gone to Pennsylvania, and I was assistant scout master at the time, and I went with them, and one of the other fellows who, I don't believe that he went into the service, he had a car and took a chance, we drove back to Cleveland because I had, I had got a gasoline ration when I was home on furlough, and so, we drove back to Cleveland and went to the parade in downtown Cleveland. END OF SIDE ONE BEGIN SIDE TWO

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: That was bad, I bumped into some people that I knew and just a lot of milling around and people were happy and that type of thing, just basically, like you see the guy kissing the nurse and stuff like that. You kissed a lot of people that you didn't know, that type of thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were in uniform I assume?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Lot of kisses?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Oh, yeah. My brother, who was discharged before I was. He came from the Pacific, he had civilian clothes and Richmond Brothers on Euclid Avenue were selling suits, $29.95, I think it was, to G.I.'s only. You had to bring your discharge with you and you could buy a suit, one suit and a white shirt. And I went there, my buddy and I went there, we each got a suit, and we each got a white shirt. And my brother was trying to get us through Sears or where ever, couldn't get anything, he didn't want to bother with that. I don't know if that's the best suit I ever had, by golly to be able to get a brand new suit when the guys didn't go into service couldn't get one and some of the those did couldn't get one, herringbone twill, blue. I don't have it anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Well, yes, one time when one of the fellows said to me that, we're dug in, right next to a hedge row, which were about five foot high, he thought there were Germans on the other side. I climbed up and looked, no German tanks along the road, which were within six feet of me. And so I went back to the lieutenant, I told him, I said those are German tanks and there's troops sleeping on top of them. I said, we have to get out of here. And he said no, those are our tanks. And I said, lieutenant, I've been here too long, those are German soldiers, those are German tanks. I'm pulling my squad out, you can do as you please. He said he would court martial me. Second time. And I pulled my squad out and ended up that the whole platoon followed, including the lieutenant, and they were German tanks. So, instead of court martialling me he gave me a bronze star. That sticks out in my memory because in the German army, I think they would have stayed there when daylight came, they would have been annihilated. The orders had to come from the top, not middle level management. Another time I had to go up to Pill Box, it was company headquarters, and I had to go there for something and a lot of shelling going on and hand to hand combat, very close. Lieutenant came in and asked if we had a mortar, and I said yes. He said he needed mortar fire, and I said, okay, tell me where. Well, he told me where and stuff like that, I couldn't get anybody else to man the guns; so, I had to set it myself and fire it. The range was so close they were afraid to throw hand grenades and I dropped the shells where he wanted them, practically straight up. If you're familiar with a mortar, you can fire straight up in the air and it will come straight down and have the wind shift, I could have blown myself up. He came back and said, did a good job and everything. And I blew his ear off with one of my mortar shells. That's how close his men were to the enemy. So, he gave me a bronze star, too. At least nobody else had gone out and fired a gun. There's little things that you don't think of for fifty years, you know. I've going to have a headache after this.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other decorations or things that you can tell me about?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Well, I got the combat infantry badge, three unit citations and good conduct and stuff like that. Three bronze stars altogether.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You never told me how you got the third one?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I don't remember. All I know is that it's on my records, and when I was discharged from the hospital, they were very thorough and went through everything. I'm a states service officer for the military order for the Purple Heart. Now, find out a lot of guys got discharged, didn't file claims, didn't check their decorations, in a hurry to get home. Being in a hospital, I was in no hurry, and they did a wonderful job for me. I got all my records that were available to me and my decorations, my pay and everything, and my claim, everything was handled very well. Here's people fifty years later that should have been getting money for the last fifty, fifty-five years, and now trying to find the records after the fire in St. Louis and that type of thing and try to find somebody that remembers you getting shot or breaking a leg or whatever, it's very, very difficult.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, how did they award the combat infantry badge at that point?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: As far as qualifications?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Un-huh?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: You had to be an infantry man and you had to have been in combat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, that basically after your first combat action?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: You were eligible. And I believe no one over the rank of colonel could get it, it was basically enlisted mans thing. Now, I belonged to the Combat Infantry Association and now they're talking about the people with the medical infantry badge, should they join us. Well, that's a controversy on both sides, you know, they were there, but, they weren't infantry. They have a different badge, it paid ten dollars a month; so, that's an award you really tried to get. You didn't try to get the Purple Heart, but that was awarded. I have a lot of people ask me how I won it. I had the wrong number in the lottery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, were you squad leader the whole time that you were over there?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: From Hill 122, I would say, oh, awarded on the 5th of July, 5th of July on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, what was your job basically before that?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I had to pick up a target, if it wasn't designated to me, estimate the range. When you found out where the first round landed, you had to traverse right or left or fire further out, closer or whatever, and that had to be done by my own way of figuring how far we were from the enemy, whether it's five hundred yards or six hundred yards. If I figured five hundred, and we fired at Atlanta hundred yards behind them, I knew that I had to bring them in two terms or whatever, and, sideways was by degrees, that's why I was trying to use that German range finder to help myself?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So this is for mortars?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: .60 millimeter mortar. So, I can't remember, I tried to think back and I can't remember ever firing three or four times, and I know in eight months I had to fire a lot longer than that, but it's all, it's all easy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Not that I can think of.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was D-Day kept a big secret before you went in?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: We were in town -- I should go back to that. When we moved from Wales down to England, we're on the coast, and it was an area that was under heavy camouflage and we had to stay in our tents all day. In the evening we could go outside. We could go to the mess hall and they showed movies all day long, but you couldn't be observed outside with a camouflage was you could go one way or the other and that was about it. And that was in the artillery range of the French coast. And forgetting the airplanes, they could get us in trouble. We stayed there probably a week and then we went through town, and we were loaded on to a boat, I can't remember the size or anything, and we went out to a LCI, landing craft infantry, and we went aboard. There's two hundred, we were over strength company, of course, and there were two hundred or two hundred and ten of us, and we got on there, one of the sailors says you might as well take your stuff off. No, we are going back. No, you're not getting off until you get to France. That's how we found out we were ready for the invasion. We were there and found out, must have been two hundred and ten of us or two, twenty, and only bunks for two hundred. So we had ten or twenty guys on guard duty, walking around the boat, all for the five, six days that we were on that boat, and, we were running out of rations and with the invasion being postponed, they thought that we might have to go back to England to get food. Well, it ended up, as you know, that they went on the 6th instead of the 5th. I'd say I spent seven days out on the English Channel kind of going around in a circle in that weather because they had five thousand or fifty-five hundred, depending on who you quote, boats out there that had to get over there and they had to coordinate. That was a big job, getting all of that coordinated. We didn't realize it at the time, but I'll never forget coming across the channel and seeing all the boats, primarily boats behind us or in front of us with barrage balloons on the front and the stern so that the strafing planes could not get down too low, and we were all milling around, circling or whatever until they got everything in line in order to go in. And one talk I gave, the principal of Normandy High School mentioned it, about the barrage balloons in England. Well, the joke then was that they cut the barrage balloons loose, England would sink into the ocean. But they had them to keep the planes from coming in under two hundred feet or hundred feet, whatever it was. But, I forgot all about these barrage balloons, but the principal had come in at D plus two or three and he saw them. So, a lot of times I speak at schools, and there's two of us, one says something and it brings something to mind. Had you been there, you know, we would have had a lot more to say because you remember things as it's brought to your mind.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good, excellent. I think we've covered it, the question -- oh, when you finally got back, I guess you were, you came back to a hospital. Do you remember the reunion with your family when you got back stateside?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I got, you want this?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I ended up at Halloran General Hospital on Long Island, and I called home, that's when I saw my first television set, and I told my folks that I was only going to be there a short period of time and while they were going to try to make arrangements from Cleveland to get up to see me, I told them to wait. I did have relatives in Brooklin, New York, and I called them and they did come out to see me. I saw them a day or two before I left the states and a day or two after I got back to the states. And my folks called and told me that they were coming up, and stuff, and well, I had to have surgery and all that. And that's when I was in West Virginia, they were going to come and I told them not to come because I didn't want them to see me weighing hundred and something pounds and with a plate in my head. My head wrapped up and stuff like that with the stitches still in it; so, I didn't see my family until I came home on furlough, which was, oh, when would that be, I came back in March. I was back here when they took the Ramagon Bridge where Roosevelt died. I was back in the states for that; so, it had to be maybe April or May of '45, I saw my folks. '45, yeah, it would be '45. I got out in '46. So, that's the first I saw my folks. I didn't want them to see me like that. A lot of guys did. I remember one fellow in the hospital, he had a hole in the front of his forehead, you could put a baseball in, and very erratic. He could play the piano beautifully, but whatever he played the first thing in the morning, he couldn't play anything else all day. And they told him that he had to shave, well, when he finally did, after he got hollered at enough times, he shaved one side of his face and walked by the nurses station, showed them he shaved, he didn't shave the other side. And I thought this was an old guy, and his wife came up to visit him, found out that he was in his twenties but he looked and acted like he was fifty-five. Now, his mind was whatever lobe in the brain was completely lost right up over the right eye. I met a lot of people that were a heck of a lot worst off than I was and some that weren't, but, you think of those who are the worst off. I go to the Drexel Hospital for bingo for the patients once a month, and have occasion to go to Wake Park Hospital three times next week, and I get to see a lot of the guys that are still in hospitals and ailing from that. I see a lot of gold bricks that never were overseas, but the government is taking care of their aids or whatever, but, I can't, I can't do anything about that. It bothers me to go out there and see people being taken care of by the government for the drug and alcohol abuse, in with combat veterans, it kind of goes against the grain. Your probably familiar with Patton slapping a soldier. Well, if he felt he was a goldbrick, he didn't belong with combat wounded. You're not suppose to hit them, I realize. You shot them, he might be better off, but we're all human, we have our own pride. If you weren't there and you weren't doing your job, nobody was hitting you with kid gloves. I still feel that way. Anything else under general?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you didn't have any close encounters with Patton, did you?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Yes, when I was taken from the hospital, taken up to the St. Vivth area, there's a sign saying St. Vivth, 6 kilometers, something like that, there was a jeep sitting there, and I recognize it, it was a generals' car and stars on it, and I think it was a major or lieutenant colonel came over and asked me why I didn't have a helmet and why I didn't have a rifle, and I explained they took me out of the hospital and sent me up there as is. He went back over and explained to General Patton, and he waved and drove away, and that was my only encounter with him. But, I have met his son, General Patton, his daughter in-law, his two granddaughters, one granddaughter is a mother superior of a Catholic Order of nuns in Conneticut and two of the generals, well, they would be great nieces and nephews, in my travels. So, so, I kind of agree with most of what Patton had to say. I read great many books on it, and I think that he had the right idea to get in there and get it done, don't fight a defensive war. They did that in World War II, and they gained very little ground, and they didn't really finish the war and they lost a lot of men. We lost a lot of men, but we did it and we took entire countries, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany and France; so, I think we've accomplished what we've set out to do, just fortunate to be back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good, unless you can think of anything else, like you said -- I've?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Oh, I will by the time you get to the end of the street. I have done this a number of times, try to keep, you said to keep it in order, trying to keep it in order, your mind don't work that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And I know some things that you will remember later and that's fine. As far as the old history tape, that's the way they always work, very rarely. I'll get a guy that will be in order for ten minutes.

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I wanted to mention the Battle of the Bulge and part of our meeting, these are designated, whoever comes up and talk, his experience, and you can tell greatly what type outfit the guy was in by his experience. If he's talking about, well, the hot food was late and the beds were lumpy and my jeep wouldn't start, he wasn't a rifleman. And other guys get up and tell a completely different story of being tickled to death to have cold food and sleeping in the side of a barn instead of on the outside, and, I think it helps the organization. We get about thirty to forty guys at that meeting and they come from, quite a few of them from the Euclid area, they come from different parts of the state. Other organizations were lucky to get three or four to a meeting, and I think that interplay, your story is better than mine or it's different than mine and find out that really it took all of these different groups. But, one of the trips, I took one guy got up and he was talking about how great the French were, and he's going on and on, and I beg to differ with you, I says. I landed before you did and I went all through France and I don't have that opinion at all. Well, I found out why, he was a cook, regimental headquarters; so, he was five, six miles behind the line at all times. How nice the French were to him. Sure, he had food to give them, and when a French woman stuck her head out of a window with a rifle in her hand and we shot her, that's a different feeling about the French people. Look here, they're not all nice people. I didn't trust the French, why would I? If they had weapons. They lived four years with the Germans, and as an example in Luxembourg we stayed in the house in closing the Bulge, and they wouldn't talk to us, they didn't want us because we had already taken that ground, then got pushed out and taken it again, they're afraid to fraternize with us, the Germans might come back. They made fun of us because the Germans came and pushed us out with horse drawn vehicles, artillery pieces, stuff. And we had trucks, that we were inferior to the Germans, they didn't trust us and consequently we didn't trust them. One other thing we did, bring to mind. We did, when Patton ran out of gasoline, they shipped it all out to the first British Army, and we were put on out post, I think two mortars and two machine guns were put out on a outpost and we were told, we were given ten and one rations to make them last because we don't have anymore gas to bring anymore food and we stayed out in that wide open area, no combat, but we stayed there for a week, two weeks, and the farmer fed us, rabbits or whatever and that was a case of, we had nothing to do except keep our eyes opened, but we got to know that French family. I'm sorry now, this young girl maybe eight years old, I didn't get her name and address and stuff like that. But you don't think of those things, being over there later could have contacted them and that type of thing. Missed a lot of opportunities, but hindsight is very very good. But that was a situation, they didn't have gasoline, so, you just eat your rations and hang on to some because it might be a long tomorrow. One of the fellows got a Purple Heart with me in a different chapter, lives in Warren, and we see each other at district meetings, he's a state chaplain. And told him that we had a veterans of Battle of Bulge group; so, he drove up, he and his wife come to our meetings. He wasn't at the last one, he didn't give an invocation. A lot of people go to great lengths to come to that and that was a small battle overall, but, people were interested in that one, and Ed Stock, as an example, that's when they first went into combat, there was, at our meetings probably half the guys, that's when they saw their first action and that's why when they had the dedication at the Stone, you knew about the dedication of Stone at Writman?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I knew about it, I haven't seen it, no.

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Well, one of our fellows did all that work and donated, he's a stone mason or whatever and -- where was I going?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: About the dedication ceremony?

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they decided to have it on June the 6th, so they said we should have somebody talk on D-Day. So, I sat in the front seat with my head down, one smart aleck in the back said, George was there. So, I gave a talk out there and funny, Battle of the Bulge group to speak on D-Day, because that's what I was asked to speak on, and most of the guys have no knowledge of France at all. Their whole war started either in Belgium, Luxembourg or Germany, and I didn't realize how many replacements had come up and went into battle that late in the year. Now in Ambrose book he list the different organizations and when they landed and stuff like that. And a lot of outfits came in the last minute. Had I stayed in the 63rd Division, theoretically, I would have seen 21 days of combat. They came over at the end of the war, but probably the chance to sign all the guys I was in had already gone, but as a division they came, I think it was 21 days of combat instead of our division is credited with 310. Yes, I did pick up more than a little things as far as I have a Nazi flag, which is probably twenty by fourteen, twenty by eight, whatever the ratio comes out. I liberated that from a post office and found a saw and I cut the flag pole off. I couldn't bring the pole home. And that, and the German insignia on the mask of the flag, I mailed both of those back to my then girlfriend and a sword, different small things, arm bands, pins from German soldiers. I sent that back, and when we broke up, she gave me all that, I still have it. I take it to schools and lay it out and try to explain it. V-mail is something that people don't know anything about, now it's not to far from the fax machine, but it's a different era, people never heard of anything like that. There's so much of War World II, things of that nature that people don't know anything about. Radios were completely different and all, but nothing large, I never -- well, I did have a .25 millimeter Czechoslovakian handgun pistol, but the medics took that away from me at the aids station when they rifled through, went through everything I owned. I did have postage stamps that were unissued, uncirculated, I should say, still in books an inch thick, they took those too. Anything of value they kind of relieved me of. But, they're people too. I tried to shoot them, but the chaplain talked me out of that because I had my .45, but I was blind at the time and he wasn't sure who I would shoot, I guess. I was not exactly a shrinking violet. But, coming out of high school I was in very good physical shape. Like I said earlier, our gym teacher gave us, called a senior gym, and it was nothing unusual after strenuous gym period to do 25 pushups and then go out and run two miles or three miles, which put us in pretty good shape; so, I did very well in the infiltration course and the obstacle course. My platoon leader, I forgot, was from Balden Wallace, he played football for Balden Wallace and I did so well on the obstacle course that he challenged me. The only problem was, I had already run it once, and he hadn't; so, he beat me by a few steps, see, I ran track and cross country in high school. But, you find some nice things. I did get to meet his wife, she came down for Christmas when we were still down in Van Dorn, Mississippi, he was killed, he evidently went to another outfit, he was killed, I know that, but I never had any contact with his family or anything; so I'm not looking for any people anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think we got it now.

sp.speaker: George T. Doyle
sp.p: I think we got it.
